title: 20 days of compute vs 7 hours: rethinking what state-of-the-art means — Bertrand Charpentier, Pruna
talk_summary: Pruna's Bertrand Charpentier argues that 'state of the art' is not a single model: public leaderboards disagree, are built on too few samples, and are dominated by large foundation models, while internal manual inspection is biased by few samples and personal preference. He advocates evaluating on many samples under real use-case conditions, using multiple task-specific metrics, and choosing models from a Pareto front of quality vs. latency/cost rather than maximizing quality alone.

takeaways.technique: Pareto-front model selection instead of single 'best' model
takeaways.what_they_do: Plot candidate models on quality (y) vs. an efficiency axis (latency or price, x) and only consider models on the Pareto front; multiple models are 'state of the art' depending on the efficiency/quality tradeoff you want.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is not one single state of the art model, but there are actually multiple of them
takeaways.numbers: Quality scores clustered ~1100-1200 Elo while efficiency varied up to ~20x faster

takeaways.technique: Task-specific eval sets, not aggregate benchmarks
takeaways.what_they_do: Build leaderboards per concrete use case (object removal, text rendering, etc.) because rankings differ completely per task and no model wins everywhere; pick the model that wins on your actual task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you focus on removing objects, look at this leaderboard and not the others

takeaways.technique: Evaluate on many samples under production conditions
takeaways.what_they_do: Warn that leaderboards use only a few thousand samples and that win rates are never near 100%, so if your use case falls in the 40% of losses you pick the wrong model; average over many samples close to the final setup.
takeaways.evidence_quote: most of the models they lose at least 40% of their of their battles
takeaways.numbers: Leaderboards built on a few thousand samples; top models lose >=40% of pairwise battles

takeaways.technique: Multiple metrics with known semantics; distrust tiny deltas
takeaways.what_they_do: Show that a single standard metric (CLIP score) gives inconsistent rankings with tiny variations across models, while a task-appropriate metric gives consistent, significant separation; insist on understanding what each metric measures and using several.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's important to understand what you actually measured with this
takeaways.numbers: CLIP-score variations between models were 'super small'; task-specific metric gave clear separation

takeaways.technique: Scale human/LLM-judge evaluation to avoid single-rater bias
takeaways.what_they_do: Demonstrate that manual inspection is biased both by the inspector and by the few samples seen (people changed preferences between rounds); human eval is good but must be scaled across many raters and samples.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you are two times biased by you and by also the number of samples

takeaways.technique: Treat efficiency as a first-class selection axis
takeaways.what_they_do: Quantify the full evaluation cost of the top model (20 days compute, $5k, 556 kWh) vs. an efficient alternative (7 hours, $265) and argue the marginal quality gain often isn't worth the compute.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the additional gain you get with quality is not worth the efficiency the the the compute cost
takeaways.numbers: 20 days / $5k / 556 kWh vs 7 hours / $265 for the same evaluation volume
